# 0. Why this project exists, and why it is a strong project

Read this before you install anything. If you can explain this page in your own words, you can explain the whole project in an interview.

## The problem in one paragraph

Cummins sells engines that run in trucks, mines, ships and generators. Modern engines are full of sensors (temperatures, pressures, speeds) and send readings over the network all the time. When an engine wears out and fails in the field, it is expensive: the truck stops, the customer loses money, a technician has to travel, and the failure may become a **warranty claim**. If you can see an engine **getting worse before it fails**, you can plan maintenance instead of reacting to a breakdown. That is called **predictive maintenance**.

To do it, a company needs a **data pipeline**: a system that takes the sensor readings as they arrive, cleans them, keeps them safely, computes an **engine health score**, and raises an **alert** early enough to act. That pipeline must be reliable: no readings lost, no readings counted twice, bad data must not break it, and it must recover if a machine crashes.

**This project builds exactly that pipeline, on real public engine data, on your laptop, for free.**

## What you will have at the end

- A **live stream** of 200 jet engines (NASA's public C-MAPSS dataset, every engine run until it failed) replayed as if the engines were flying right now.
- **Kafka** receiving the readings, **Spark Structured Streaming** processing them, **Delta Lake** tables storing them in three layers (**bronze → silver → gold**).
- A **health score** per engine and **alerts** (WARNING, then CRITICAL) that fire a median of **44 cycles (flights) before failure** for **every one** of the 200 engines.
- **Proof** that nothing is lost or duplicated even when you inject duplicates, late messages and broken messages **and kill the processing program in the middle** (`kill -9`): 54,787 expected events, 54,787 stored, 0 missing, 0 duplicates.
- A **dead-letter table** where every bad message is kept with a reason, instead of crashing the pipeline.
- A **load test** that measures how fast it is and finds the bottleneck.
- **Unit tests**, a **CI pipeline** on GitHub, a **dashboard**, and **documentation** (architecture, decisions, a failure log).

## Why this is a good project (what a reviewer sees)

Most student data projects are "read a CSV, transform it, write a CSV". They show you can use a library. They do not show you can run something in production. This project is designed to show production thinking:

| What most projects show | What this project shows | Why an interviewer cares |
|---|---|---|
| A pipeline that runs once | A pipeline that **keeps running**, survives a crash and resumes exactly where it stopped | Real pipelines fail every week. Recovery is the job. |
| "It works" | "It works, **and here is the proof**" (a manifest of every event compared with the output) | Claims are cheap. Verification is rare and convincing. |
| Clean input | Input with **duplicates, late data and garbage** injected on purpose | Real sources are dirty. Handling it is most of data engineering. |
| One script | **Layers** (bronze/silver/gold) with clear jobs | This is how Databricks lakehouses at Cummins-sized companies are organised. |
| No numbers | **Measured** throughput, latency percentiles, a found bottleneck, a capacity plan | Shows you can reason about scale with evidence. |
| No mistakes shown | **16 documented failures** with cause and fix | Shows debugging skill and honesty. |
| Random fake data | **Real NASA data**, public and verifiable | Anyone can check your results. |
| A model that "looks right" | A model **evaluated per fleet** that revealed a 44% miss on one fault type, then fixed it (56% → 100%) | Shows you check results by segment, not just on average. |

## Why it fits the Cummins Data Engineer 1 posting

| Posting line | Where this project covers it |
|---|---|
| Ingest **event-based** data | Kafka producer and consumer, partitions, keys |
| Build reliable, scalable pipelines **with monitoring and alerts** | Streaming queries, checkpoints, progress metrics, alerts table, report command |
| Monitor and troubleshoot **data quality and integrity** | Validation rules, dead-letter table with reason codes, exactly-once verification |
| **Spark, Kafka**, big data open source | Spark Structured Streaming, Kafka, Delta Lake |
| **Physical data models** and storage architecture | Bronze/silver/gold tables, partitioning, table grains |
| **Testing and troubleshooting** | 14 unit tests, a parity test, a crash test, a load test, the failure log |
| **IoT technology** | Engine telemetry, event time, late data, per-device ordering |
| **AI-ready data** | Clean per-cycle features and labels suitable for failure prediction models |
| **DevOps / CI** | Docker, GitHub Actions CI |

## Why each big choice was made (short version, details in each chapter)

- **Streaming instead of batch:** engines send data continuously and alerts are only useful if they are early. A nightly batch job would warn a day late.
- **Kafka:** the standard way companies move events between systems. It stores messages for days, so you can replay them, and it keeps each engine's readings in order. (Azure Event Hubs, which Cummins is likely to use, speaks the same Kafka protocol.)
- **Spark Structured Streaming:** the same engine data teams already use for batch on Databricks, so one skill covers both. It has checkpoints for crash recovery.
- **Delta Lake:** turns plain files into reliable tables (no half-written files, updates with MERGE, history). It is the default table format on Databricks.
- **Bronze/silver/gold:** keep the raw data untouched (so you can always rebuild), clean it once, and serve business-ready tables.
- **NASA C-MAPSS data:** real engines run until failure, public, no login, and the right domain (engines) for Cummins. Never use employer data in a personal project.
- **Everything local and free:** anyone can run it with Docker and Python, no cloud account, no cost. The same code runs on Databricks by changing paths.

## How to use this guide

1. Do the chapters **in order**. Each one ends with a **Check** step: do not continue until the check passes.
2. Every file is given **complete**. Create the file with exactly that name and content. Read the explanation under it before moving on; that is what you will be asked about.
3. Every technology has a box: **What it is, Why here, Alternatives, Advantages, Impact**. Learn those boxes; they are your interview answers.
4. When something breaks, look at the **Troubleshooting** chapter first: the same errors happened when this project was first built.
5. Type the code where you can instead of only copying it. Typing makes you read every line.

**Time needed:** about 2-3 days for a first build if you are new, plus a day to run the tests and write your own notes.

**An honest note on ownership:** after you build this yourself following the guide, you can truthfully say you built and verified it. In an interview, be ready to explain any line and any decision; if you followed a guide for parts of it, say so plainly and focus on what you understood, changed and measured yourself. Interviewers respect that far more than a claim that falls apart under questions.

# 1. The big picture, and the words you need

## The flow, in plain words

```
NASA data file ──► Producer (Python) ──► Kafka topic ──► Spark: Bronze ──► Silver ──► Gold ──► Dashboard
 200 engines       sends one reading     a durable        raw copy       clean,       health,     charts
 run to failure    per engine per tick   queue/log        of everything  checked,     alerts,
                   (+ chaos on purpose)                                   no dupes     fleet stats
                                                           Silver ──► Dead-letter table (bad messages + reason)
```

1. A **producer** program reads the NASA file and sends one JSON message per engine reading into **Kafka**, as if 200 engines were flying right now. On purpose, it also sends some duplicates, late messages and broken messages.
2. **Spark** reads Kafka continuously in small batches every 5 seconds (**micro-batches**).
3. **Bronze** stores every message exactly as received.
4. **Silver** checks each message. Good ones are parsed into columns, de-duplicated and given a health score. Bad ones go to a **dead-letter** table with a reason.
5. **Gold** keeps one row per engine (latest health, alert level), an alerts table (each alert once), and per-minute fleet statistics.
6. A **report/verify** command proves nothing was lost or duplicated. A **dashboard** shows the fleet.

## Words you must know (one line each)

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Event / message** | One reading from one engine for one cycle, as JSON |
| **Cycle** | One flight of the engine. Engines live 128-362 cycles in this data |
| **Producer / consumer** | A program that writes to / reads from Kafka |
| **Topic** | A named stream in Kafka (ours: `engine-telemetry`) |
| **Partition** | A topic is split into partitions so several readers work in parallel. Order is kept **inside** a partition |
| **Key** | A value attached to each message (ours: `engine_id`). Same key → same partition → that engine's readings stay in order |
| **Offset** | The position number of a message inside a partition |
| **Micro-batch** | Spark processes whatever arrived in the last few seconds as one small batch |
| **Checkpoint** | A folder where Spark records what it has processed, so after a crash it continues from there |
| **Delta table** | A folder of Parquet files plus a transaction log that makes it behave like a reliable database table |
| **Bronze / silver / gold** | Raw → clean → business-ready layers (the "medallion" pattern) |
| **Dead-letter table** | Where bad records go, with the reason, instead of being dropped or crashing the job |
| **Event time** | When the reading happened (set by the producer), as opposed to when we received it |
| **Watermark** | How long Spark waits for late events before treating a time period as complete |
| **Idempotent** | Doing it twice gives the same result as once. The key to safe retries |
| **Exactly-once** | Every event affects the result exactly one time, even with retries and crashes |
| **EWMA** | A smoothed average that gives more weight to recent values; used to smooth the noisy health score |
| **MERGE (upsert)** | Update the row if the key exists, insert if not |

## The final folder layout (you will create all of it)

```
turbofan-telemetry/
  requirements.txt  docker-compose.yml  Dockerfile  .gitignore  README.md
  telemetry/
    __init__.py  config.py  cmapss.py  events.py  admin.py  producer.py  spark.py  report.py  cli.py
    jobs/  __init__.py  bronze.py  silver.py  gold.py  run.py
  tests/  test_events.py  test_spark_parity.py
  scripts/  calibrate.py  demo.sh  loadtest.py
  dashboard/  app.py
  docs/  architecture.md  decisions.md  build-log.md  capacity-plan.md
  .github/workflows/ci.yml
  data/   lake/   (created by the programs, never committed to Git)
```

**Check:** you can explain, without looking, what bronze, silver and gold each do, and why the message key is the engine id.

# 2. Set up your computer

You need five tools. Install them once.

| Tool | Version | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Git | any recent | Version control, push to GitHub |
| Python | **3.12** (3.10-3.13 work) | The language of the whole project |
| Java (JDK) | **17 or 21** | Spark runs on the Java Virtual Machine, even when you write Python |
| Docker Desktop | any recent | Runs Kafka in a container, no Kafka install needed |
| VS Code | any | Editor (any editor works) |

**Windows users:** install **WSL2 with Ubuntu** (`wsl --install` in an admin PowerShell, then restart) and run every command in this guide inside the Ubuntu terminal. Spark and shell scripts are much easier there. Install Docker Desktop on Windows and enable "Use the WSL 2 based engine".

**macOS:** install Homebrew, then `brew install git python@3.12 openjdk@17` and Docker Desktop.

**Ubuntu / WSL:**

```bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y git python3.12 python3.12-venv openjdk-17-jdk
```

### Tech box: Docker
- **What it is:** a tool that runs software in isolated "containers" built from images, so it behaves the same on every machine.
- **Why here:** Kafka is a Java server with many settings. With Docker you start a correct, pinned Kafka with one command and delete it just as easily.
- **Alternatives:** installing Kafka by hand (slow, error-prone), a cloud Kafka (needs an account and money).
- **Advantages:** reproducible, no system clutter, the same file works for every reviewer.
- **Impact:** without it, "works on my machine" problems would eat days.

### Tech box: Java for a Python project
- **What it is:** Spark is written in Scala and runs on the JVM. PySpark is a Python front end that talks to that JVM.
- **Why it matters:** if Java is missing or the wrong version, Spark will not start (`JAVA_HOME is not set`, `UnsupportedClassVersionError`).
- **Rule:** Spark 4 needs Java 17 or 21.

## Check that everything works

```bash
git --version
python3 --version        # 3.12.x (3.10-3.13 fine)
java -version            # 17 or 21
docker info              # must print "Server Version". If it errors, open Docker Desktop (daemon not running)
```

## Create the project folder and a virtual environment

```bash
mkdir turbofan-telemetry && cd turbofan-telemetry
git init
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate          # Windows WSL is the same. Your prompt now starts with (.venv)
mkdir -p telemetry/jobs tests scripts dashboard docs .github/workflows
touch telemetry/__init__.py telemetry/jobs/__init__.py
```

### Tech box: virtual environment (venv)
- **What:** a private folder of Python packages for this project only.
- **Why:** this project pins exact versions (Spark 4.0.1 etc.). Installing them globally can break other projects, and other projects can break this one.
- **Alternatives:** conda, poetry, uv. venv is built into Python and enough here.
- **Impact:** without it, the "Python workers use the wrong interpreter" bug (F9 in Troubleshooting) is much more likely.

## requirements.txt

Create `requirements.txt`:

```text
pyspark==4.0.1
delta-spark==4.0.0
confluent-kafka==2.8.0
pandas==2.2.3
pyarrow==19.0.1
deltalake==0.25.5
streamlit==1.41.1
pytest==8.3.4
```

**Every line explained:**

| Package | What it does here | Why this one |
|---|---|---|
| `pyspark==4.0.1` | The stream processor | Spark 4 supports Python 3.13 and Java 17/21. Spark 3.5 does not support Python 3.13 (F4) |
| `delta-spark==4.0.0` | Delta Lake for Spark | Delta versions are built for one Spark version: 4.0.0 matches Spark 4.0 |
| `confluent-kafka==2.8.0` | Python Kafka client (producer, admin) | Built on librdkafka (C): much faster than `kafka-python` and supports the idempotent producer |
| `pandas==2.2.3`, `pyarrow==19.0.1` | Used by Spark's `applyInPandas` in gold, and by the report | pandas UDFs move data with Arrow |
| `deltalake==0.25.5` | delta-rs: reads Delta tables **without Spark** | The report, verify and dashboard start in milliseconds instead of waiting for a JVM |
| `streamlit==1.41.1` | Dashboard | A web dashboard in one Python file |
| `pytest==8.3.4` | Tests | The standard Python test runner |

**Why pin exact versions (`==`)?** So the project behaves the same next year. Spark, Delta and the Kafka connector must match each other exactly; an unpinned upgrade is the most common reason a data project stops working.

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

## .gitignore

Create `.gitignore`:

```text
data/
lake/
.venv/
__pycache__/
*.pyc
spark-warehouse/
metastore_db/
derby.log
.pytest_cache/
```

`data/` and `lake/` are created by the programs (downloaded data, Delta tables, checkpoints). They are large, machine-specific and reproducible, so they never go into Git.

**Check:** `python -c "import pyspark, delta, confluent_kafka; print(pyspark.__version__)"` prints `4.0.1`.

# 3. Run Kafka with Docker

### Tech box: Apache Kafka
- **What it is:** a distributed, durable **log** of events. Producers append messages to a topic; consumers read them at their own pace; messages stay for a retention period (ours: 7 days) whether or not they were read.
- **Why here:** engines produce a continuous stream. Kafka absorbs bursts, keeps each engine's readings in order (by key), lets several consumers read the same data, and lets you **replay** after a bug or crash.
- **Alternatives:** **Azure Event Hubs** / AWS Kinesis (managed cloud versions; Event Hubs even speaks the Kafka protocol, so this code works against it), RabbitMQ (a queue: messages are deleted once consumed, no replay), writing files to a folder (no ordering, no backpressure, slow).
- **Advantages:** replay, ordering per key, parallelism through partitions, huge throughput, industry standard.
- **Impact:** without a durable log, a crash in the processor would lose whatever was in flight, and you could not reprocess history.

### Tech box: KRaft mode
Old Kafka needed a second system, **ZooKeeper**, to manage the cluster. Since Kafka 3.3 it can manage itself with its own consensus protocol (**KRaft**), and **Kafka 4.0 removed ZooKeeper completely**. So we run one container that is both broker and controller. Simpler, and current.

Create `docker-compose.yml`:

```yaml
# Local stack: Kafka (KRaft mode, no ZooKeeper) + Kafka UI. No accounts or logins needed.
#   docker compose up -d          -> Kafka on localhost:9092, Kafka UI on http://localhost:8080
# The optional `app` and `dashboard` services run the Python/Spark code in a container,
# so you don't need Java or Python installed locally (see README, "Option B").
services:
  kafka:
    image: apache/kafka:3.9.0
    container_name: tt-kafka
    ports:
      - "9092:9092"
    environment:
      KAFKA_NODE_ID: 1
      KAFKA_PROCESS_ROLES: broker,controller
      KAFKA_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://:19092,PLAINTEXT_HOST://:9092,CONTROLLER://:9093
      KAFKA_ADVERTISED_LISTENERS: PLAINTEXT://kafka:19092,PLAINTEXT_HOST://localhost:9092
      KAFKA_LISTENER_SECURITY_PROTOCOL_MAP: CONTROLLER:PLAINTEXT,PLAINTEXT:PLAINTEXT,PLAINTEXT_HOST:PLAINTEXT
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_QUORUM_VOTERS: 1@kafka:9093
      KAFKA_CONTROLLER_LISTENER_NAMES: CONTROLLER
      KAFKA_INTER_BROKER_LISTENER_NAME: PLAINTEXT
      KAFKA_OFFSETS_TOPIC_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1
      KAFKA_TRANSACTION_STATE_LOG_MIN_ISR: 1
      KAFKA_GROUP_INITIAL_REBALANCE_DELAY_MS: 0
      KAFKA_AUTO_CREATE_TOPICS_ENABLE: "false"
      KAFKA_LOG_RETENTION_HOURS: 168
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "/opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --list >/dev/null 2>&1"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 10

  kafka-ui:
    image: provectuslabs/kafka-ui:v0.7.2
    container_name: tt-kafka-ui
    depends_on: [kafka]
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      KAFKA_CLUSTERS_0_NAME: local
      KAFKA_CLUSTERS_0_BOOTSTRAPSERVERS: kafka:19092

  # ---- Option B: run the code inside Docker (no local Java/Python needed) ----
  app:
    build: .
    profiles: ["app"]
    depends_on: [kafka]
    working_dir: /app
    volumes:
      - .:/app
      - ivy-cache:/root/.ivy2          # Spark's downloaded Kafka/Delta jars survive restarts
    environment:
      KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP: kafka:19092
    ports:
      - "4040:4040"                    # Spark UI
    entrypoint: ["python", "-m", "telemetry.cli"]

  dashboard:
    build: .
    profiles: ["app"]
    working_dir: /app
    volumes:
      - .:/app
    ports:
      - "8501:8501"
    command: ["streamlit", "run", "dashboard/app.py", "--server.address=0.0.0.0", "--server.headless=true"]

volumes:
  ivy-cache:
```

**What each important setting means:**

| Setting | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `image: apache/kafka:3.9.0` | Official Apache image, **pinned** version. Never use `latest` in a project others must reproduce |
| `KAFKA_PROCESS_ROLES: broker,controller` | One node does both jobs (KRaft, no ZooKeeper) |
| `KAFKA_LISTENERS` / `ADVERTISED_LISTENERS` | Kafka gives clients an address to reconnect to. `localhost:9092` for programs on your laptop, `kafka:19092` for programs inside Docker. Getting this wrong is the #1 "cannot connect to Kafka" problem |
| `*_REPLICATION_FACTOR: 1` | We have one broker, so internal topics can only have one copy. In production: 3 |
| `KAFKA_AUTO_CREATE_TOPICS_ENABLE: "false"` | Topics must be created on purpose (with our partition count). Prevents typos silently creating new topics |
| `KAFKA_LOG_RETENTION_HOURS: 168` | Keep messages 7 days, so you can replay |
| `healthcheck` | Docker knows when Kafka is really ready |
| `kafka-ui` | A web page to look inside Kafka (topics, partitions, messages) |
| `app`, `dashboard` with `profiles: ["app"]` | Optional: run the Python code inside Docker if you cannot install Java/Python (Option B, chapter 17). Not started by default |

```bash
docker compose up -d
docker compose ps          # tt-kafka should be "healthy" after ~20-30 s
```

Open **http://localhost:8080**: Kafka UI. There are no topics yet.

**Check:** `docker compose ps` shows `tt-kafka` healthy and Kafka UI loads in the browser.

# 4. Get and understand the NASA data ### Tech box: NASA C-MAPSS - **What it is:** NASA simulated turbofan (jet) engines with a physics model called C-MAPSS. Every engine starts healthy and runs until it fails. One row = one cycle (≈ one flight): engine number, cycle number, 3 operating settings and 21 sensor readings. - **Why here:** real engine degradation, public and free (no login), small (12 MB), widely used in predictive-maintenance research, and in Cummins' domain (engines). - **Alternatives:** random fake data (no real signal to find, so the alerts would mean nothing), employer data (**never**: confidential), Kaggle copies (need a login). - **Impact:** because the data is real, your "44 cycles of warning" result is a real, checkable finding. **The four subsets:** | Subset | Engines | Operating conditions | Fault types | |---|---|---|---| | **FD001** | 100 | 1 | 1 (high-pressure compressor, "HPC") | | FD002 | 260 | 6 | 1 | | **FD003** | 100 | 1 | 2 (HPC **and** fan) | | FD004 | 248 | 6 | 2 | **We use FD001 + FD003.** They run at one operating condition, so when a sensor drifts, it is because of wear. In FD002/FD004 the same sensor value means different things at different altitudes and speeds, so you would first need per-condition normalisation (a good extension later). ## The data module You will create `telemetry/cmapss.py`. It has one job: **get the NASA data and turn it into Python dictionaries**. First the walkthrough, piece by piece, then the complete file to copy. ### Walkthrough: `telemetry/cmapss.py` **1. The docstring and imports** ```python """Download and parse NASA's C-MAPSS turbofan engine degradation dataset. Source: NASA Prognostics Center of Excellence data repository (public, no login). Each row = one operating cycle (flight) of one engine, run until failure. Columns: unit, cycle, 3 operational settings, 21 sensor readings. """ import io import random import urllib.request import zipfile from .config import DATA_DIR ``` - The text in triple quotes at the top is a **module docstring**: the first thing anyone (and `help()`) reads. Always say what a file does and where its data comes from. - `io`, `random`, `urllib.request`, `zipfile` are all in Python's **standard library**: nothing to install. `urllib.request` downloads, `zipfile` opens zip archives, `io.BytesIO` lets us treat bytes in memory as if they were a file. - `from .config import DATA_DIR`: the dot means "from the **same package**" (`telemetry`). This is a **relative import**. It works because the folder has an `__init__.py`, which makes it a package. > **Python lesson: modules and packages.** A `.py` file is a **module**. A folder with `__init__.py` is a **package**. You run code inside a package with `python -m telemetry.cli` (the `-m` flag), never `python telemetry/cli.py`, or relative imports like `from .config` fail with "attempted relative import with no known parent package". **2. Constants** ```python URL = "https://phm-datasets.s3.amazonaws.com/NASA/6.+Turbofan+Engine+Degradation+Simulation+Data+Set.zip" SENSORS = [f"s{i}" for i in range(1, 22)] COLUMNS = ["unit", "cycle", "op_setting_1", "op_setting_2", "op_setting_3"] + SENSORS # FD001 and FD003 run at a single operating condition, so sensor drift = wear. # (FD002/FD004 mix six conditions and would need per-condition normalisation.) DEFAULT_SUBSETS = ("FD001", "FD003") ``` - `URL`: the official NASA Prognostics Center mirror. The `+` signs are URL-encoded spaces. The first link tried (data.nasa.gov) was dead (F3): pin the source and document it. - `SENSORS = [f"s{i}" for i in range(1, 22)]` is a **list comprehension** that builds `["s1", "s2", ..., "s21"]`. `range(1, 22)` stops **before** 22. - `COLUMNS` is the order of values on each line of the file: unit, cycle, 3 settings, 21 sensors (26 numbers). - Names in `CAPITALS` are **constants** by convention: set once, never changed. **3. `download()`: fetch once, extract** ```python def download(force: bool = False) -> None: """Fetch the zip once and extract train_FD00x.txt files into data/cmapss/.""" out = DATA_DIR / "cmapss" if (out / "train_FD001.txt").exists() and not force: print(f"already present: {out}") return out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) print(f"downloading {URL} ...") with urllib.request.urlopen(URL, timeout=120) as r: outer = zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(r.read())) inner_name = next(n for n in outer.namelist() if n.endswith("CMAPSSData.zip")) inner = zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(outer.read(inner_name))) for name in inner.namelist(): if name.endswith(".txt"): (out / name).write_bytes(inner.read(name)) print(f"extracted to {out}") ``` - `out = DATA_DIR / "cmapss"`: `DATA_DIR` is a `pathlib.Path`, and `/` joins paths safely on every operating system. - The `if ... exists() and not force: return` line makes the function **idempotent**: running it twice does not download twice. You will see this idea everywhere in data engineering. - `urlopen(URL, timeout=120)`: always set a **timeout** on network calls, or a stuck connection hangs your program forever. - The NASA zip contains **another zip** (`CMAPSSData.zip`). `next(n for n in ... if n.endswith(...))` finds the first matching name: a **generator expression** inside `next()`. - `(out / name).write_bytes(...)` writes each `.txt` file. **4. `load()`: text lines → dictionaries** ```python def load(subset: str) -> list[dict]: """Rows of train_.txt as dicts. Falls back to synthetic data if the file is missing.""" path = DATA_DIR / "cmapss" / f"train_{subset}.txt" if not path.exists(): print(f"{path} not found: using synthetic engines (run `python -m telemetry.cli download` for real NASA data)") return synthetic(subset) rows = [] for line in path.read_text().split("\n"): parts = line.split() if not parts: continue vals = [float(x) for x in parts[: len(COLUMNS)]] row = dict(zip(COLUMNS, vals)) row["unit"], row["cycle"] = int(row["unit"]), int(row["cycle"]) rows.append(row) return rows ``` - Each line looks like `1 1 -0.0007 -0.0004 100.0 518.67 641.82 ...`: numbers separated by spaces. `line.split()` (no argument) splits on any run of whitespace and ignores trailing spaces. - `dict(zip(COLUMNS, vals))` pairs each column name with its value: `{"unit": 1.0, "cycle": 1.0, "op_setting_1": -0.0007, ...}`. `zip` walks two lists side by side. - `unit` and `cycle` are converted back to `int` because they are identifiers and counters, not measurements. - If the file is missing, it **falls back** to `synthetic(subset)` and says so. The project still runs offline. > **Engineering lesson: design a fallback for every external dependency.** Links move, APIs go down. A fallback with the same shape keeps development and tests moving, and the message makes the downgrade visible instead of silent. **5. `synthetic()`: fake engines with the same shape** ```python _BASE = {"s1": 518.67, "s2": 642.38, "s3": 1586.9, "s4": 1402.8, "s5": 14.62, "s6": 21.61, "s7": 553.95, "s8": 2388.06, "s9": 9055.8, "s10": 1.3, "s11": 47.36, "s12": 521.9, "s13": 2388.05, "s14": 8137.4, "s15": 8.418, "s16": 0.03, "s17": 392.3, "s18": 2388.0, "s19": 100.0, "s20": 38.93, "s21": 23.36} _DRIFT = {"s2": 1.3, "s3": 16, "s4": 28, "s7": -2.6, "s9": 43, "s11": 0.84, "s12": -2.2, "s14": 31, "s15": 0.105, "s17": 4.5, "s20": -0.53, "s21": -0.31} def synthetic(subset: str, engines: int = 100, seed: int = 7) -> list[dict]: """Engines whose degrading sensors drift exponentially toward failure, same shape as C-MAPSS.""" rnd = random.Random(f"{subset}-{seed}") rows = [] for unit in range(1, engines + 1): life = rnd.randint(128, 360) for cycle in range(1, life + 1): wear = (cycle / life) ** 3 row = {"unit": unit, "cycle": cycle, "op_setting_1": rnd.gauss(0, 0.002), "op_setting_2": rnd.gauss(0, 0.0003), "op_setting_3": 100.0} for s in SENSORS: noise = abs(_BASE[s]) * 0.0008 if s in _DRIFT else 0 row[s] = round(_BASE[s] + _DRIFT.get(s, 0) * wear + rnd.gauss(0, noise), 4) rows.append(row) return rows ``` - `_BASE` holds each sensor's healthy average and `_DRIFT` how far it moves by end of life (+ rises, − falls). The leading `_` means "internal, not for other modules". - `random.Random(f"{subset}-{seed}")` creates a **seeded** random generator: the same seed gives the same "random" engines every time, so tests are repeatable. - `wear = (cycle / life) ** 3`: wear grows slowly at first and fast near the end, like real degradation. - `rnd.gauss(0, noise)` adds small normally distributed noise, like a real sensor.
Complete telemetry/cmapss.py to copy ```python """Download and parse NASA's C-MAPSS turbofan engine degradation dataset. Source: NASA Prognostics Center of Excellence data repository (public, no login). Each row = one operating cycle (flight) of one engine, run until failure. Columns: unit, cycle, 3 operational settings, 21 sensor readings. """ import io import random import urllib.request import zipfile from .config import DATA_DIR URL = "https://phm-datasets.s3.amazonaws.com/NASA/6.+Turbofan+Engine+Degradation+Simulation+Data+Set.zip" SENSORS = [f"s{i}" for i in range(1, 22)] COLUMNS = ["unit", "cycle", "op_setting_1", "op_setting_2", "op_setting_3"] + SENSORS # FD001 and FD003 run at a single operating condition, so sensor drift = wear. # (FD002/FD004 mix six conditions and would need per-condition normalisation.) DEFAULT_SUBSETS = ("FD001", "FD003") def download(force: bool = False) -> None: """Fetch the zip once and extract train_FD00x.txt files into data/cmapss/.""" out = DATA_DIR / "cmapss" if (out / "train_FD001.txt").exists() and not force: print(f"already present: {out}") return out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) print(f"downloading {URL} ...") with urllib.request.urlopen(URL, timeout=120) as r: outer = zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(r.read())) inner_name = next(n for n in outer.namelist() if n.endswith("CMAPSSData.zip")) inner = zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(outer.read(inner_name))) for name in inner.namelist(): if name.endswith(".txt"): (out / name).write_bytes(inner.read(name)) print(f"extracted to {out}") def load(subset: str) -> list[dict]: """Rows of train_.txt as dicts. Falls back to synthetic data if the file is missing.""" path = DATA_DIR / "cmapss" / f"train_{subset}.txt" if not path.exists(): print(f"{path} not found: using synthetic engines (run `python -m telemetry.cli download` for real NASA data)") return synthetic(subset) rows = [] for line in path.read_text().split("\n"): parts = line.split() if not parts: continue vals = [float(x) for x in parts[: len(COLUMNS)]] row = dict(zip(COLUMNS, vals)) row["unit"], row["cycle"] = int(row["unit"]), int(row["cycle"]) rows.append(row) return rows # Baseline means used by the synthetic generator (from healthy FD001 cycles) _BASE = {"s1": 518.67, "s2": 642.38, "s3": 1586.9, "s4": 1402.8, "s5": 14.62, "s6": 21.61, "s7": 553.95, "s8": 2388.06, "s9": 9055.8, "s10": 1.3, "s11": 47.36, "s12": 521.9, "s13": 2388.05, "s14": 8137.4, "s15": 8.418, "s16": 0.03, "s17": 392.3, "s18": 2388.0, "s19": 100.0, "s20": 38.93, "s21": 23.36} _DRIFT = {"s2": 1.3, "s3": 16, "s4": 28, "s7": -2.6, "s9": 43, "s11": 0.84, "s12": -2.2, "s14": 31, "s15": 0.105, "s17": 4.5, "s20": -0.53, "s21": -0.31} def synthetic(subset: str, engines: int = 100, seed: int = 7) -> list[dict]: """Engines whose degrading sensors drift exponentially toward failure, same shape as C-MAPSS.""" rnd = random.Random(f"{subset}-{seed}") rows = [] for unit in range(1, engines + 1): life = rnd.randint(128, 360) for cycle in range(1, life + 1): wear = (cycle / life) ** 3 row = {"unit": unit, "cycle": cycle, "op_setting_1": rnd.gauss(0, 0.002), "op_setting_2": rnd.gauss(0, 0.0003), "op_setting_3": 100.0} for s in SENSORS: noise = abs(_BASE[s]) * 0.0008 if s in _DRIFT else 0 row[s] = round(_BASE[s] + _DRIFT.get(s, 0) * wear + rnd.gauss(0, noise), 4) rows.append(row) return rows ```
It needs `config.py` for the `DATA_DIR` path. Create `telemetry/config.py` now (every setting is explained in chapter 5):
Complete telemetry/config.py to copy ```python """Central configuration. Override anything with environment variables.""" import os from pathlib import Path ROOT = Path(os.environ.get("TT_ROOT", Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1])) DATA_DIR = ROOT / "data" LAKE = Path(os.environ.get("TT_LAKE", ROOT / "lake")) BOOTSTRAP = os.environ.get("KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP", "localhost:9092") TOPIC = os.environ.get("TT_TOPIC", "engine-telemetry") PARTITIONS = int(os.environ.get("TT_PARTITIONS", "6")) # Delta tables (bronze / silver / gold) and their streaming checkpoints TABLES = { "bronze": LAKE / "bronze" / "telemetry_raw", "silver": LAKE / "silver" / "telemetry", "dlq": LAKE / "silver" / "dead_letter", "engine_state": LAKE / "gold" / "engine_current_state", "alerts": LAKE / "gold" / "engine_alerts", "fleet_minute": LAKE / "gold" / "fleet_health_minute", } CHECKPOINTS = LAKE / "_checkpoints" # Streaming behaviour WATERMARK = os.environ.get("TT_WATERMARK", "10 minutes") # how late an event may arrive TRIGGER = os.environ.get("TT_TRIGGER", "5 seconds") # micro-batch interval MAX_OFFSETS_PER_TRIGGER = int(os.environ.get("TT_MAX_OFFSETS", "200000")) # backpressure cap ```
> **Python lesson: `pathlib` and environment variables.** `Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]` means "the folder above the folder this file is in", which is the project root wherever you run from. `os.environ.get("TT_LAKE", default)` reads an environment variable if set, otherwise uses the default. That is how one codebase runs on a laptop, in Docker and in the cloud without edits. Download the data: ```bash python -c "from telemetry import cmapss; cmapss.download()" ls data/cmapss # train_FD001.txt ... train_FD004.txt, test_*, RUL_* ``` ## Look at the data yourself (do this, it is where the design comes from) ```bash python - <<'EOF' from statistics import mean from telemetry.cmapss import load, SENSORS rows = load("FD001") by = {} for r in rows: by.setdefault(r["unit"], []).append(r) first = [rs[0] for rs in by.values()]; last = [max(rs, key=lambda r: r["cycle"]) for rs in by.values()] print("engines:", len(by), "| life (cycles) min/avg/max:", min(len(v) for v in by.values()), round(mean(len(v) for v in by.values())), max(len(v) for v in by.values())) for s in SENSORS: a, b = mean(r[s] for r in first), mean(r[s] for r in last) print(f"{s:>4} first cycle {a:10.3f} last cycle {b:10.3f} {'RISES' if b > a * 1.0005 else 'FALLS' if b < a * 0.9995 else 'flat'}") EOF ``` **What you will see** (this is what the health score is built on): - Engines live **128-362 cycles**, about 206 on average. - **s1, s5, s6, s10, s16, s18, s19** are flat: no information, ignored. - **s2, s3, s4, s11, s15, s17 rise** as the engine wears (temperatures and pressures go up). - **s7, s12, s20, s21 fall**. - **s8, s9, s13, s14** are the fan and core **speed** sensors. s9 and s14 also rise, s8 and s13 barely move. The project leaves the four speed sensors out and builds the score from the **10 temperature, pressure and flow sensors** above, which drift cleanly with wear. (Trying the speed sensors in the score is a good experiment once everything works: measure it with the calibration script in chapter 7.) That table is the whole idea of the health score in chapter 5: measure how far the 10 drifting sensors have moved from their healthy values. **Check:** the script prints 100 engines and you can name which sensors rise and which fall.

# 5. Configuration, the event contract and the health logic This chapter is pure Python: no Kafka, no Spark. It holds the **rules** of the system: what an event looks like, what makes it valid, how health is computed, when to alert. Keeping rules separate from the big tools is the best design decision in the project. The rules can be tested in milliseconds and reused by Spark, the tests and the calibration script. ## config.py (created in chapter 4) Every path, name and tuning number lives in one place, and each can be overridden with an environment variable (for example `TT_TRIGGER="1 second"`). | Setting | Value | Why | |---|---|---| | `TOPIC` / `PARTITIONS` | `engine-telemetry`, 6 | 6 partitions → up to 6 parallel readers: enough for a laptop, few enough to see in Kafka UI | | `TABLES` | bronze, silver, dlq, three gold tables | Each Delta table is a folder under `lake/` | | `CHECKPOINTS` | `lake/_checkpoints` | One sub-folder per streaming query. It is the query's memory: never share it between queries, never delete it casually | | `WATERMARK` | 10 minutes | How late an event may arrive and still be de-duplicated | | `TRIGGER` | 5 seconds | Micro-batch interval: a balance between delay and overhead | | `MAX_OFFSETS_PER_TRIGGER` | 200,000 | **Backpressure**: after an outage, Spark catches up in batches of at most 200k instead of swallowing hours at once | ## events.py, walked through **1. Imports and the version** ```python """Event contract and pure domain logic (no Spark, no Kafka): unit-testable in milliseconds.""" import json import math import uuid from datetime import datetime, timezone from .cmapss import SENSORS SCHEMA_VERSION = 1 NAMESPACE = uuid.UUID("6f1d6a2e-2b6a-4f7e-9a51-3c1b2b9d7e10") ``` - `json` turns Python dicts into text and back. `math` is used for `isnan`. `uuid` makes IDs. `datetime, timezone` give timestamps with a time zone. - `SCHEMA_VERSION = 1` goes into every event, so a future format change can be detected by readers. - `NAMESPACE` is a fixed UUID used to generate **deterministic** event IDs (explained in 3). **2. The health-score constants** ```python HEALTH_SENSORS = { "s2": (+1, 642.3832, 0.3795), "s3": (+1, 1586.8985, 4.6482), "s4": (+1, 1402.831, 5.9308), "s7": (-1, 553.9477, 0.6237), "s11": (+1, 47.3561, 0.1769), "s12": (-1, 521.9049, 0.5068), "s15": (+1, 8.4184, 0.0264), "s17": (+1, 392.27, 1.1424), "s20": (-1, 38.9323, 0.1296), "s21": (-1, 23.3592, 0.0787), } # C-MAPSS FD003 has a SECOND fault mode (fan degradation). Its signature differs from the HPC fault above: # s7, s12, s20, s21 rise instead of falling and s15 falls instead of rising (build-log F14, Milestone T1). FAN_SIGNS = {"s2": +1, "s3": +1, "s4": +1, "s7": +1, "s11": +1, "s12": +1, "s15": -1, "s17": +1, "s20": +1, "s21": +1} # The fan pattern moves s7/s12 by 20+ standard deviations, so it is down-weighted to give the same lead times and # false-alarm rate as the HPC pattern. Tuned on odd FD003 engines, checked on even ones (scripts/calibrate.py). FAN_WEIGHT = 0.4 ``` - `HEALTH_SENSORS` maps each of the 10 drifting sensors to a **tuple** `(direction, healthy_mean, healthy_std)`. Example: `"s2": (+1, 642.3832, 0.3795)` means s2 rises with wear, is about 642.38 when healthy, and normally wobbles by about 0.38. - Those means and standard deviations were measured from the first 30 cycles (healthy) of every FD001 engine. - `FAN_SIGNS` is the second failure pattern: for fan faults, five sensors move the other way. - `FAN_WEIGHT = 0.4` scales the fan pattern down so it does not alarm too early (chapter 7 shows how it was chosen). > **Python lesson: tuples and dicts.** A tuple `(a, b, c)` is a fixed, ordered group of values. You unpack it in one line: `sign, mu, sd = HEALTH_SENSORS["s2"]`. A dict maps keys to values; `.items()` gives `(key, value)` pairs to loop over. **3. Valid ranges, alert policy and IDs** ```python SENSOR_RANGES = {s: (0.0, 20000.0) for s in SENSORS} SENSOR_RANGES.update({"s11": (40.0, 60.0), "s4": (1200.0, 1600.0), "s2": (600.0, 700.0)}) # Alert policy, calibrated on FD001 run-to-failure data (see docs/decisions.md, ADR-004): EWMA_ALPHA = 0.2 WARNING_AT = 1.5 # median lead ~44 cycles before failure CRITICAL_AT = 2.5 # median lead ~19 cycles before failure LEVELS = {0: "OK", 1: "WARNING", 2: "CRITICAL"} def engine_id(subset: str, unit: int, loop: int = 0) -> str: return f"{subset}-{unit:03d}" + (f"-L{loop}" if loop else "") def event_id(engine: str, cycle: int) -> str: """Deterministic: the same engine+cycle always gets the same id, so duplicates are detectable.""" return str(uuid.uuid5(NAMESPACE, f"{engine}:{cycle}")) ``` - `SENSOR_RANGES`: every sensor allowed 0-20,000 by default, then tighter ranges for three sensors (`.update` overwrites those keys). Values outside are **physically impossible**, so they mean a broken sensor or a transport error. - `EWMA_ALPHA = 0.2`, `WARNING_AT = 1.5`, `CRITICAL_AT = 2.5`: the alert policy (chapter 7). - `engine_id("FD001", 7, 2)` → `"FD001-007-L2"`. `{unit:03d}` pads with zeros to 3 digits so IDs sort nicely. The `-L2` suffix is added only for replay loops 1+. - `uuid.uuid5(NAMESPACE, "FD001-007:113")` always returns the **same** UUID for the same text. A random `uuid4()` would give a new ID each time. > **Why deterministic IDs matter.** If the same reading is sent twice, both copies carry the same ID, so the duplicate can be found anywhere downstream. With random IDs a resend looks like a new event, and "exactly-once" is impossible to check. This one line is the foundation of the whole dedupe and verify story. **4. Building and serialising an event** ```python def make_event(subset: str, row: dict, loop: int = 0, now: datetime | None = None) -> dict: eng = engine_id(subset, row["unit"], loop) now = now or datetime.now(timezone.utc) return { "schema_version": SCHEMA_VERSION, "event_id": event_id(eng, row["cycle"]), "fleet": subset, "engine_id": eng, "cycle": int(row["cycle"]), "event_time": now.isoformat(timespec="milliseconds").replace("+00:00", "Z"), "op_settings": [row["op_setting_1"], row["op_setting_2"], row["op_setting_3"]], "sensors": {s: row[s] for s in SENSORS}, } def to_bytes(event: dict) -> bytes: return json.dumps(event, separators=(",", ":")).encode() ``` - `now = now or datetime.now(timezone.utc)`: use the time passed in (tests pass a fixed time) or the current UTC time. Passing time in makes the function **testable**. - `isoformat(timespec="milliseconds").replace("+00:00", "Z")` gives `2026-11-25T08:00:00.000Z`, the standard ISO 8601 UTC format. - `to_bytes` uses `separators=(",", ":")` to remove spaces: smaller messages. Kafka sends **bytes**, so the string is `.encode()`d (UTF-8). One event looks like this: ```json {"schema_version": 1, "event_id": "6c1f...", "fleet": "FD001", "engine_id": "FD001-007", "cycle": 113, "event_time": "2026-11-25T14:56:44.621Z", "op_settings": [0.0007, -0.0004, 100.0], "sensors": {"s1": 518.67, "s2": 642.1, "...": "...", "s21": 23.4}} ``` > **Tech box: JSON for events.** *Why:* readable, every tool understands it, easy to debug in Kafka UI. *Alternatives:* **Avro / Protobuf** with a schema registry: binary, several times smaller, schema checked on every send. That is the production choice at scale. *Impact here:* ~900 bytes per event; the capacity plan notes the switch for large fleets. **5. Validation with reason codes** ```python def validate(event: dict | None) -> str | None: """Return None if valid, else a dead-letter reason code. Mirrors the Spark silver rules.""" if not isinstance(event, dict): return "MALFORMED_JSON" for f in ("event_id", "engine_id", "cycle", "event_time", "sensors"): if event.get(f) in (None, ""): return "MISSING_FIELD" sensors = event["sensors"] for s in SENSORS: v = sensors.get(s) if v is None or (isinstance(v, float) and math.isnan(v)): return "MISSING_FIELD" lo, hi = SENSOR_RANGES[s] if not lo <= v <= hi: return "OUT_OF_RANGE" return None ``` - Returns `None` for a good event, or a **reason code** string. The order of checks matters: first "is it even a dict?", then required fields, then every sensor present, then every sensor in range. - `event.get(f) in (None, "")` treats missing and empty the same. - `isinstance(v, float) and math.isnan(v)`: NaN (not a number) is a float that is not equal to itself, so it needs `math.isnan`. - `lo <= v <= hi` is Python's **chained comparison**. Why reason codes and not just "bad"? You can count, chart and route them: "154 missing fields from one gateway" tells you where to look. The **same rules** are rewritten in Spark in silver (chapter 12) and a test proves both agree. **6. The health score** ```python def _index(sensors: dict, signs: dict) -> float: total = 0.0 for s, (_, mu, sd) in HEALTH_SENSORS.items(): total += signs[s] * (sensors[s] - mu) / sd return total / len(HEALTH_SENSORS) HPC_SIGNS = {s: sign for s, (sign, _, _) in HEALTH_SENSORS.items()} def hpc_index(sensors: dict) -> float: """Signed z-score average for the HPC (compressor) fault pattern.""" return _index(sensors, HPC_SIGNS) def fan_index(sensors: dict) -> float: """Signed z-score average for the fan fault pattern.""" return _index(sensors, FAN_SIGNS) def health_index(sensors: dict) -> float: """Fault-mode aware health index (v2): the worse of the HPC and fan patterns. ~0 when healthy, rises with wear of either kind. v1 used only the HPC pattern, so fan-fault engines cancelled themselves out and 44% of FD003 never alerted (build-log F14). """ return max(hpc_index(sensors), FAN_WEIGHT * fan_index(sensors)) def fault_mode(sensors: dict) -> str: """Which pattern dominates: useful for routing the alert to the right maintenance team.""" return "FAN" if FAN_WEIGHT * fan_index(sensors) > hpc_index(sensors) else "HPC" ``` In plain words, `_index` does, for each of the 10 sensors: 1. `(sensors[s] - mu) / sd`: how many "normal wobbles" away from healthy the reading is (a **z-score**). 2. multiply by the direction sign, so wear always pushes the number **up**; 3. average the 10 values. Result: about **0 for a healthy engine**, rising as it wears. `hpc_index` uses the compressor directions, `fan_index` the fan directions, and `health_index` takes `max(hpc, 0.4 × fan)`: the worse of the two. `fault_mode` says which pattern won, so an alert can be routed to the right team. Worked example: if s2 reads 643.14 → (643.14 − 642.38) / 0.38 ≈ +2.0. If all 10 sensors were 2 wobbles toward wear, the index would be 2.0, above WARNING (1.5). **7. State and alerts: `advance_state`** ```python def level_for(ewma: float) -> int: return 2 if ewma >= CRITICAL_AT else 1 if ewma >= WARNING_AT else 0 def advance_state(prev: dict | None, events: list[dict]) -> tuple[dict | None, list[dict]]: """Fold a batch of one engine's events into its state. Returns (new_state, alerts_raised). - Events are applied in cycle order. - Events at or before the last applied cycle are ignored: this makes re-processing a micro-batch (after a crash) idempotent, and drops stale out-of-order cycles. - An alert is raised only when the level escalates (OK->WARNING, ->CRITICAL). """ state = dict(prev) if prev else None alerts = [] for e in sorted(events, key=lambda x: x["cycle"]): if state and e["cycle"] <= state["last_cycle"]: continue hi = e["health_index"] ewma = hi if not state else EWMA_ALPHA * hi + (1 - EWMA_ALPHA) * state["ewma_health"] prev_level = state["alert_level"] if state else 0 lvl = max(prev_level, level_for(ewma)) # levels only escalate until maintenance resets the engine state = {"engine_id": e["engine_id"], "fleet": e["fleet"], "last_cycle": e["cycle"], "last_event_time": e["event_time"], "health_index": hi, "ewma_health": ewma, "alert_level": lvl, "s11": e["s11"], "s4": e["s4"], "fault_mode": e.get("fault_mode")} if lvl > prev_level: alerts.append({"alert_id": f"{e['engine_id']}:{LEVELS[lvl]}", "engine_id": e["engine_id"], "fleet": e["fleet"], "level": LEVELS[lvl], "cycle": e["cycle"], "ewma_health": ewma, "event_time": e["event_time"], "fault_mode": e.get("fault_mode")}) return state, alerts ``` Read it slowly; it is the heart of the alerting: - `level_for(ewma)` maps the smoothed score to 0 (OK), 1 (WARNING) or 2 (CRITICAL) with a **conditional expression**. - `advance_state(prev, events)` takes an engine's previous state (or `None` for a new engine) and a list of its new events, and returns `(new_state, alerts)`. - `state = dict(prev) if prev else None` makes a **copy**, so the caller's dict is never changed (no hidden side effects). - `sorted(events, key=lambda x: x["cycle"])`: apply events in cycle order even if they arrived out of order. `lambda x: x["cycle"]` is a tiny unnamed function used as the sort key. - `if state and e["cycle"] <= state["last_cycle"]: continue`: **the idempotency rule**. A cycle at or before the last applied one is skipped, so replaying a batch after a crash changes nothing. - `ewma = α × new + (1 − α) × previous`: the EWMA. It needs one number of memory per engine, which is ideal for streaming. - `lvl = max(prev_level, level_for(ewma))`: levels only go **up** until maintenance; no flapping. - An alert is appended only when `lvl > prev_level`, with `alert_id = "FD001-007:WARNING"`. Each engine can raise each level once.
Complete telemetry/events.py to copy ```python """Event contract and pure domain logic (no Spark, no Kafka): unit-testable in milliseconds.""" import json import math import uuid from datetime import datetime, timezone from .cmapss import SENSORS SCHEMA_VERSION = 1 NAMESPACE = uuid.UUID("6f1d6a2e-2b6a-4f7e-9a51-3c1b2b9d7e10") # Sensors that drift with wear, and their direction (+1 rises, -1 falls as the engine degrades). # Baselines = mean / std of the first 30 (healthy) cycles of every FD001 engine. HEALTH_SENSORS = { "s2": (+1, 642.3832, 0.3795), "s3": (+1, 1586.8985, 4.6482), "s4": (+1, 1402.831, 5.9308), "s7": (-1, 553.9477, 0.6237), "s11": (+1, 47.3561, 0.1769), "s12": (-1, 521.9049, 0.5068), "s15": (+1, 8.4184, 0.0264), "s17": (+1, 392.27, 1.1424), "s20": (-1, 38.9323, 0.1296), "s21": (-1, 23.3592, 0.0787), } # C-MAPSS FD003 has a SECOND fault mode (fan degradation). Its signature differs from the HPC fault above: # s7, s12, s20, s21 rise instead of falling and s15 falls instead of rising (build-log F14, Milestone T1). FAN_SIGNS = {"s2": +1, "s3": +1, "s4": +1, "s7": +1, "s11": +1, "s12": +1, "s15": -1, "s17": +1, "s20": +1, "s21": +1} # The fan pattern moves s7/s12 by 20+ standard deviations, so it is down-weighted to give the same lead times and # false-alarm rate as the HPC pattern. Tuned on odd FD003 engines, checked on even ones (scripts/calibrate.py). FAN_WEIGHT = 0.4 # Physically plausible ranges. Anything outside is a sensor/transport fault -> dead-letter. SENSOR_RANGES = {s: (0.0, 20000.0) for s in SENSORS} SENSOR_RANGES.update({"s11": (40.0, 60.0), "s4": (1200.0, 1600.0), "s2": (600.0, 700.0)}) # Alert policy, calibrated on FD001 run-to-failure data (see docs/decisions.md, ADR-004): EWMA_ALPHA = 0.2 WARNING_AT = 1.5 # median lead ~44 cycles before failure CRITICAL_AT = 2.5 # median lead ~19 cycles before failure LEVELS = {0: "OK", 1: "WARNING", 2: "CRITICAL"} def engine_id(subset: str, unit: int, loop: int = 0) -> str: return f"{subset}-{unit:03d}" + (f"-L{loop}" if loop else "") def event_id(engine: str, cycle: int) -> str: """Deterministic: the same engine+cycle always gets the same id, so duplicates are detectable.""" return str(uuid.uuid5(NAMESPACE, f"{engine}:{cycle}")) def make_event(subset: str, row: dict, loop: int = 0, now: datetime | None = None) -> dict: eng = engine_id(subset, row["unit"], loop) now = now or datetime.now(timezone.utc) return { "schema_version": SCHEMA_VERSION, "event_id": event_id(eng, row["cycle"]), "fleet": subset, "engine_id": eng, "cycle": int(row["cycle"]), "event_time": now.isoformat(timespec="milliseconds").replace("+00:00", "Z"), "op_settings": [row["op_setting_1"], row["op_setting_2"], row["op_setting_3"]], "sensors": {s: row[s] for s in SENSORS}, } def to_bytes(event: dict) -> bytes: return json.dumps(event, separators=(",", ":")).encode() def validate(event: dict | None) -> str | None: """Return None if valid, else a dead-letter reason code. Mirrors the Spark silver rules.""" if not isinstance(event, dict): return "MALFORMED_JSON" for f in ("event_id", "engine_id", "cycle", "event_time", "sensors"): if event.get(f) in (None, ""): return "MISSING_FIELD" sensors = event["sensors"] for s in SENSORS: v = sensors.get(s) if v is None or (isinstance(v, float) and math.isnan(v)): return "MISSING_FIELD" lo, hi = SENSOR_RANGES[s] if not lo <= v <= hi: return "OUT_OF_RANGE" return None def _index(sensors: dict, signs: dict) -> float: total = 0.0 for s, (_, mu, sd) in HEALTH_SENSORS.items(): total += signs[s] * (sensors[s] - mu) / sd return total / len(HEALTH_SENSORS) HPC_SIGNS = {s: sign for s, (sign, _, _) in HEALTH_SENSORS.items()} def hpc_index(sensors: dict) -> float: """Signed z-score average for the HPC (compressor) fault pattern.""" return _index(sensors, HPC_SIGNS) def fan_index(sensors: dict) -> float: """Signed z-score average for the fan fault pattern.""" return _index(sensors, FAN_SIGNS) def health_index(sensors: dict) -> float: """Fault-mode aware health index (v2): the worse of the HPC and fan patterns. ~0 when healthy, rises with wear of either kind. v1 used only the HPC pattern, so fan-fault engines cancelled themselves out and 44% of FD003 never alerted (build-log F14). """ return max(hpc_index(sensors), FAN_WEIGHT * fan_index(sensors)) def fault_mode(sensors: dict) -> str: """Which pattern dominates: useful for routing the alert to the right maintenance team.""" return "FAN" if FAN_WEIGHT * fan_index(sensors) > hpc_index(sensors) else "HPC" def level_for(ewma: float) -> int: return 2 if ewma >= CRITICAL_AT else 1 if ewma >= WARNING_AT else 0 def advance_state(prev: dict | None, events: list[dict]) -> tuple[dict | None, list[dict]]: """Fold a batch of one engine's events into its state. Returns (new_state, alerts_raised). - Events are applied in cycle order. - Events at or before the last applied cycle are ignored: this makes re-processing a micro-batch (after a crash) idempotent, and drops stale out-of-order cycles. - An alert is raised only when the level escalates (OK->WARNING, ->CRITICAL). """ state = dict(prev) if prev else None alerts = [] for e in sorted(events, key=lambda x: x["cycle"]): if state and e["cycle"] <= state["last_cycle"]: continue hi = e["health_index"] ewma = hi if not state else EWMA_ALPHA * hi + (1 - EWMA_ALPHA) * state["ewma_health"] prev_level = state["alert_level"] if state else 0 lvl = max(prev_level, level_for(ewma)) # levels only escalate until maintenance resets the engine state = {"engine_id": e["engine_id"], "fleet": e["fleet"], "last_cycle": e["cycle"], "last_event_time": e["event_time"], "health_index": hi, "ewma_health": ewma, "alert_level": lvl, "s11": e["s11"], "s4": e["s4"], "fault_mode": e.get("fault_mode")} if lvl > prev_level: alerts.append({"alert_id": f"{e['engine_id']}:{LEVELS[lvl]}", "engine_id": e["engine_id"], "fleet": e["fleet"], "level": LEVELS[lvl], "cycle": e["cycle"], "ewma_health": ewma, "event_time": e["event_time"], "fault_mode": e.get("fault_mode")}) return state, alerts ```
**Check:** you can explain why `event_id` must be deterministic, and what `advance_state` does when the same batch is applied twice.

# 6. Unit tests first > **Tech box: pytest.** *What:* Python's standard test runner: functions named `test_*` containing `assert`. *Why here:* the rules in `events.py` decide whether alerts are right, and testing them needs no Kafka or Spark, so tests run in a fraction of a second after every change. *Alternatives:* `unittest` (built in, more boilerplate); testing only end to end (slow, and a failure does not tell you which rule broke). *Impact:* the "replay is idempotent" test is your crash-safety proof, written as code. ### Walkthrough: `tests/test_events.py` **1. Fixtures as plain values** ```python """Fast unit tests of the pure domain logic (no Spark, no Kafka).""" import json from datetime import datetime, timezone import pytest from telemetry import cmapss from telemetry.events import (CRITICAL_AT, WARNING_AT, advance_state, event_id, health_index, make_event, to_bytes, validate) ROW = cmapss.synthetic("FD001", engines=1)[0] NOW = datetime(2026, 11, 25, 8, 0, tzinfo=timezone.utc) def ev(cycle, hi, engine="FD001-001"): ``` - `ROW` is one synthetic healthy reading; `NOW` a fixed time so outputs are predictable. - `ev(cycle, hi)` builds a minimal event dict for `advance_state`. Small helper functions like this keep tests short and readable. **2. Simple asserts** ```python def test_event_id_is_deterministic(): assert event_id("FD001-001", 5) == event_id("FD001-001", 5) assert event_id("FD001-001", 5) != event_id("FD001-001", 6) def test_make_event_roundtrip_is_valid(): e = make_event("FD001", ROW, now=NOW) assert e["engine_id"] == "FD001-001" and e["event_time"] == "2026-11-25T08:00:00.000Z" assert validate(json.loads(to_bytes(e))) is None ``` - `assert a == b` passes silently or fails with the values shown. That is all pytest needs. - The round-trip test makes an event, serialises it, parses it back and checks it is valid: it catches the producer and the validator disagreeing. **3. One test, many cases: `parametrize`** ```python @pytest.mark.parametrize("mutate,reason", [ (lambda e: None, "MALFORMED_JSON"), (lambda e: {k: v for k, v in e.items() if k != "engine_id"}, "MISSING_FIELD"), (lambda e: {**e, "sensors": {**e["sensors"], "s11": -1.0}}, "OUT_OF_RANGE"), ]) def test_validate_reasons(mutate, reason): assert validate(mutate(make_event("FD001", ROW, now=NOW))) == reason ``` - `@pytest.mark.parametrize` runs the same test three times with different inputs. Each case is reported separately. - The `lambda` functions **mutate** a good event into a bad one: `None` (malformed), without `engine_id` (missing), with `s11 = -1.0` (out of range). `{**e, "sensors": {...}}` copies a dict and overrides one key. **4. Testing behaviour, not code** ```python def test_state_escalates_and_raises_each_alert_once(): events = [ev(1, 0.0), ev(2, 0.0), ev(3, 10.0), ev(4, 10.0), ev(5, 10.0), ev(6, 10.0)] state, alerts = advance_state(None, events) assert [a["level"] for a in alerts] == ["WARNING", "CRITICAL"] assert state["alert_level"] == 2 and state["last_cycle"] == 6 assert state["ewma_health"] >= CRITICAL_AT > WARNING_AT def test_replaying_a_batch_is_idempotent(): s1, a1 = advance_state(None, [ev(1, 0.0), ev(2, 9.0), ev(3, 9.0)]) s2, a2 = advance_state(s1, [ev(1, 0.0), ev(2, 9.0), ev(3, 9.0)]) # same batch again after a crash assert s2 == s1 and a2 == [] ``` - Escalation: health jumps to 10 → exactly two alerts, WARNING then CRITICAL. - **Replay:** apply a batch, then the **same batch again** → state unchanged, no new alerts. This is the test that proves crash recovery cannot double-count. - **Out of order:** cycles 3, 1, 2 → applied in order; a stale cycle 2 arriving later is ignored. **5. Guarding the FD003 fix** ```python def _shift(pattern_signs, z): """A healthy row with every health sensor moved z standard deviations in the given pattern's direction.""" from telemetry.events import HEALTH_SENSORS row = dict(ROW) for s, (_, mu, sd) in HEALTH_SENSORS.items(): row[s] = mu + pattern_signs[s] * z * sd return row def test_fan_fault_is_detected_and_labelled(): # v1 bug (build-log F14): the fan pattern cancelled itself out in the HPC-only index. from telemetry.events import FAN_SIGNS, fault_mode, hpc_index fan_row = _shift(FAN_SIGNS, 8.0) assert hpc_index(fan_row) < WARNING_AT # the old index would miss it assert health_index(fan_row) >= CRITICAL_AT # the new one does not assert fault_mode(fan_row) == "FAN" ``` - `_shift` builds a reading where every health sensor is moved `z` standard deviations in a given pattern's direction: a synthetic "fan fault" engine. - The test asserts the **old** HPC-only index would miss it and the new index catches it and labels it FAN. If someone "simplifies" the formula later, this test fails.
Complete tests/test_events.py to copy ```python """Fast unit tests of the pure domain logic (no Spark, no Kafka).""" import json from datetime import datetime, timezone import pytest from telemetry import cmapss from telemetry.events import (CRITICAL_AT, WARNING_AT, advance_state, event_id, health_index, make_event, to_bytes, validate) ROW = cmapss.synthetic("FD001", engines=1)[0] NOW = datetime(2026, 11, 25, 8, 0, tzinfo=timezone.utc) def ev(cycle, hi, engine="FD001-001"): return {"engine_id": engine, "fleet": "FD001", "cycle": cycle, "event_time": f"t{cycle}", "health_index": hi, "s11": 47.5, "s4": 1405.0} def test_event_id_is_deterministic(): assert event_id("FD001-001", 5) == event_id("FD001-001", 5) assert event_id("FD001-001", 5) != event_id("FD001-001", 6) def test_make_event_roundtrip_is_valid(): e = make_event("FD001", ROW, now=NOW) assert e["engine_id"] == "FD001-001" and e["event_time"] == "2026-11-25T08:00:00.000Z" assert validate(json.loads(to_bytes(e))) is None @pytest.mark.parametrize("mutate,reason", [ (lambda e: None, "MALFORMED_JSON"), (lambda e: {k: v for k, v in e.items() if k != "engine_id"}, "MISSING_FIELD"), (lambda e: {**e, "sensors": {**e["sensors"], "s11": -1.0}}, "OUT_OF_RANGE"), ]) def test_validate_reasons(mutate, reason): assert validate(mutate(make_event("FD001", ROW, now=NOW))) == reason def test_health_index_near_zero_when_healthy(): assert abs(health_index(ROW)) < 1.5 def test_state_escalates_and_raises_each_alert_once(): events = [ev(1, 0.0), ev(2, 0.0), ev(3, 10.0), ev(4, 10.0), ev(5, 10.0), ev(6, 10.0)] state, alerts = advance_state(None, events) assert [a["level"] for a in alerts] == ["WARNING", "CRITICAL"] assert state["alert_level"] == 2 and state["last_cycle"] == 6 assert state["ewma_health"] >= CRITICAL_AT > WARNING_AT def test_replaying_a_batch_is_idempotent(): s1, a1 = advance_state(None, [ev(1, 0.0), ev(2, 9.0), ev(3, 9.0)]) s2, a2 = advance_state(s1, [ev(1, 0.0), ev(2, 9.0), ev(3, 9.0)]) # same batch again after a crash assert s2 == s1 and a2 == [] def test_out_of_order_events_are_applied_in_cycle_order_and_stale_ones_ignored(): s, _ = advance_state(None, [ev(3, 1.0), ev(1, 0.0), ev(2, 0.5)]) assert s["last_cycle"] == 3 s2, _ = advance_state(s, [ev(2, 99.0)]) # stale cycle arrives late assert s2 == s def test_synthetic_engines_degrade(): rows = [r for r in cmapss.synthetic("FD001", engines=1)] assert health_index(rows[-1]) > health_index(rows[0]) + 2 def _shift(pattern_signs, z): """A healthy row with every health sensor moved z standard deviations in the given pattern's direction.""" from telemetry.events import HEALTH_SENSORS row = dict(ROW) for s, (_, mu, sd) in HEALTH_SENSORS.items(): row[s] = mu + pattern_signs[s] * z * sd return row def test_fan_fault_is_detected_and_labelled(): # v1 bug (build-log F14): the fan pattern cancelled itself out in the HPC-only index. from telemetry.events import FAN_SIGNS, fault_mode, hpc_index fan_row = _shift(FAN_SIGNS, 8.0) assert hpc_index(fan_row) < WARNING_AT # the old index would miss it assert health_index(fan_row) >= CRITICAL_AT # the new one does not assert fault_mode(fan_row) == "FAN" def test_hpc_fault_is_labelled_hpc(): from telemetry.events import HPC_SIGNS, fault_mode hpc_row = _shift(HPC_SIGNS, 4.0) assert health_index(hpc_row) >= CRITICAL_AT and fault_mode(hpc_row) == "HPC" def test_alert_carries_fault_mode(): events = [{**ev(c, 10.0), "fault_mode": "FAN"} for c in range(1, 6)] _, alerts = advance_state(None, events) assert {a["fault_mode"] for a in alerts} == {"FAN"} ```
Create `tests/test_spark_parity.py` too, but **do not run it yet**: it imports the silver job you write in chapter 12, so it fails until then. It proves the Spark and Python health formulas agree. In CI, where Spark is not installed, it is skipped automatically by `pytest.importorskip("pyspark")`.
Complete tests/test_spark_parity.py to copy ```python """The silver job computes the health index in Spark; gold and the unit tests use the Python version. They must agree exactly, or alerts would differ from what was calibrated. Skipped if PySpark is not installed.""" import pytest pyspark = pytest.importorskip("pyspark") from telemetry import cmapss # noqa: E402 from telemetry.events import FAN_SIGNS, HEALTH_SENSORS, HPC_SIGNS, fault_mode, health_index # noqa: E402 @pytest.fixture(scope="module") def spark(): from pyspark.sql import SparkSession s = SparkSession.builder.master("local[1]").appName("parity").config("spark.ui.enabled", "false").getOrCreate() yield s s.stop() def test_spark_and_python_health_index_agree(spark): from telemetry.jobs.silver import fault_mode_expr, health_expr rows = cmapss.synthetic("FD001", engines=2)[:50] for signs, z in ((FAN_SIGNS, 8.0), (HPC_SIGNS, 4.0)): r = dict(rows[0]) for s, (_, mu, sd) in HEALTH_SENSORS.items(): r[s] = mu + signs[s] * z * sd rows.append(r) df = spark.createDataFrame([{k: float(v) for k, v in r.items() if k.startswith("s")} for r in rows]) got = df.select(health_expr().alias("hi"), fault_mode_expr().alias("fm")).collect() for r, g in zip(rows, got): assert g.hi == pytest.approx(health_index(r), abs=1e-9) assert g.fm == fault_mode(r) ```
Run: ```bash python -m pytest -q tests/test_events.py ``` `-q` means quiet: one dot per passing test. **Check:** all tests in `test_events.py` pass.

# 7. Calibrate the alerts on real failures Before streaming anything, find out whether the health score and thresholds actually warn **early** and **only when needed**. This runs offline on all 200 engines, cycle by cycle, with the **same functions** the stream uses. ### Walkthrough: `scripts/calibrate.py` **1. Making the project importable from a script** ```python import statistics as st import sys from collections import defaultdict from pathlib import Path sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1])) from telemetry import events # noqa: E402 from telemetry.cmapss import load # noqa: E402 EARLY = 125 # C-MAPSS engines are usually treated as healthy until ~125 cycles before failure ``` - `sys.path.insert(0, ...parents[1])` adds the project root to Python's import path, so a script in `scripts/` can `from telemetry import events`. - `# noqa: E402` tells the linter "imports after code is intentional here". - `EARLY = 125`: in C-MAPSS, engines are usually considered healthy until ~125 cycles before failure, so a warning earlier than that counts as a **false alarm**. **2. The designs being compared** ```python def old_index(s): """v1: one signed index tuned to the HPC fault (FD001).""" return sum(sign * (s[k] - mu) / sd for k, (sign, mu, sd) in events.HEALTH_SENSORS.items()) / len(events.HEALTH_SENSORS) def abs_index(s): """Alternative: mean absolute deviation (direction-agnostic).""" return sum(abs(s[k] - mu) / sd for k, (_, mu, sd) in events.HEALTH_SENSORS.items()) / len(events.HEALTH_SENSORS) DESIGNS = { "v1 signed HPC index (old)": (old_index, 1.5, 2.5), "abs deviation": (abs_index, 2.0, 3.0), "v2 max(HPC, 0.4 x fan) (new)": (events.health_index, events.WARNING_AT, events.CRITICAL_AT), ``` - `old_index` is v1 (compressor pattern only). `abs_index` ignores direction. `events.health_index` is v2. - `DESIGNS` maps a name to `(function, warning threshold, critical threshold)`. Functions are values in Python: you can store them in a dict and call them later. **3. Replaying every engine** ```python def replay(rows, index, warn, crit, alpha=events.EWMA_ALPHA): by_unit = defaultdict(list) for r in rows: by_unit[r["unit"]].append(r) out = [] for unit, rs in by_unit.items(): rs.sort(key=lambda r: r["cycle"]) last = rs[-1]["cycle"] ewma, w, c = None, None, None for r in rs: hi = index(r) ewma = hi if ewma is None else alpha * hi + (1 - alpha) * ewma if w is None and ewma >= warn: w = last - r["cycle"] if c is None and ewma >= crit: c = last - r["cycle"] out.append((unit, w, c)) return out ``` - Group rows by engine (`defaultdict(list)` creates an empty list for a new key automatically). - For each engine, walk its cycles in order, update the EWMA, and record **how many cycles before the last cycle** the WARNING and CRITICAL first fired. That number is the **lead time**. **4. Summarising** ```python def summarise(res): n = len(res) wl = [w for _, w, _ in res if w is not None] cl = [c for _, _, c in res if c is not None] p10 = lambda xs: sorted(xs)[max(0, len(xs) // 10 - 1)] if xs else None # noqa: E731 return { "engines": n, "warned": f"{len(wl)}/{n} ({100 * len(wl) // n}%)", "critical": f"{len(cl)}/{n} ({100 * len(cl) // n}%)", "warn lead median/p10": f"{st.median(wl):.0f} / {p10(wl)}" if wl else "-", "crit lead median/p10": f"{st.median(cl):.0f} / {p10(cl)}" if cl else "-", f"too early (>{EARLY})": sum(1 for w in wl if w > EARLY), } ``` - Counts engines warned, the **median** lead time (typical) and the **p10** (the worst 10%), plus warnings earlier than 125 cycles. Median and p10 say more than an average, which one outlier can drag around.
Complete scripts/calibrate.py to copy ```python """Offline alert calibration on NASA C-MAPSS run-to-failure data (Milestone T1). Replays every engine cycle by cycle through the SAME EWMA + threshold logic the stream uses, and reports for each health-index design: how many engines get a WARNING / CRITICAL before failure, how far ahead (lead time in cycles), and how many warnings are "too early" (> EARLY cycles before failure, i.e. while the engine is still healthy). python scripts/calibrate.py # compare designs on FD001 + FD003 """ import statistics as st import sys from collections import defaultdict from pathlib import Path sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1])) from telemetry import events # noqa: E402 from telemetry.cmapss import load # noqa: E402 EARLY = 125 # C-MAPSS engines are usually treated as healthy until ~125 cycles before failure def old_index(s): """v1: one signed index tuned to the HPC fault (FD001).""" return sum(sign * (s[k] - mu) / sd for k, (sign, mu, sd) in events.HEALTH_SENSORS.items()) / len(events.HEALTH_SENSORS) def abs_index(s): """Alternative: mean absolute deviation (direction-agnostic).""" return sum(abs(s[k] - mu) / sd for k, (_, mu, sd) in events.HEALTH_SENSORS.items()) / len(events.HEALTH_SENSORS) DESIGNS = { "v1 signed HPC index (old)": (old_index, 1.5, 2.5), "abs deviation": (abs_index, 2.0, 3.0), "v2 max(HPC, 0.4 x fan) (new)": (events.health_index, events.WARNING_AT, events.CRITICAL_AT), } def replay(rows, index, warn, crit, alpha=events.EWMA_ALPHA): by_unit = defaultdict(list) for r in rows: by_unit[r["unit"]].append(r) out = [] for unit, rs in by_unit.items(): rs.sort(key=lambda r: r["cycle"]) last = rs[-1]["cycle"] ewma, w, c = None, None, None for r in rs: hi = index(r) ewma = hi if ewma is None else alpha * hi + (1 - alpha) * ewma if w is None and ewma >= warn: w = last - r["cycle"] if c is None and ewma >= crit: c = last - r["cycle"] out.append((unit, w, c)) return out def summarise(res): n = len(res) wl = [w for _, w, _ in res if w is not None] cl = [c for _, _, c in res if c is not None] p10 = lambda xs: sorted(xs)[max(0, len(xs) // 10 - 1)] if xs else None # noqa: E731 return { "engines": n, "warned": f"{len(wl)}/{n} ({100 * len(wl) // n}%)", "critical": f"{len(cl)}/{n} ({100 * len(cl) // n}%)", "warn lead median/p10": f"{st.median(wl):.0f} / {p10(wl)}" if wl else "-", "crit lead median/p10": f"{st.median(cl):.0f} / {p10(cl)}" if cl else "-", f"too early (>{EARLY})": sum(1 for w in wl if w > EARLY), } def main(): data = {f: load(f) for f in ("FD001", "FD003")} cols = None print(f"| Design | Fleet | Engines | Warned | Critical | Warning lead median / p10 | Critical lead median / p10 | Warnings > {EARLY} cycles early |") print("|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|") for name, (idx, warn, crit) in DESIGNS.items(): for fleet, rows in data.items(): s = summarise(replay(rows, idx, warn, crit)) print(f"| {name} | {fleet} | " + " | ".join(str(v) for v in s.values()) + " |") if __name__ == "__main__": main() ```
```bash python scripts/calibrate.py ``` **How to read the table:** | Column | Meaning | Good value | |---|---|---| | Warned | Engines that got a WARNING before failing | 100% | | Warning lead median / p10 | Cycles of warning: typical, and worst 10% | ~44 median, ~25 p10: enough to plan maintenance | | Critical lead | Same for CRITICAL | ~17-18 | | Warnings > 125 early | Alarms while still healthy (false alarms) | Close to 0 | **What you should see:** v1 catches only **56% of FD003**; v2 catches **100% of both fleets** with the same lead time and no extra false alarms. **Why this matters (the interview story):** a model tuned on one population (FD001) silently failed on another (FD003). It was found only because the evaluation was split **per fleet**. The fan weight 0.4 was tuned on odd-numbered FD003 engines and checked on even-numbered ones, so the result is not "tuned on the test". **Try it yourself:** change `EWMA_ALPHA` to 0.1 or `WARNING_AT` to 2.0 in `events.py`, re-run, and watch lead times and false alarms move. Create the Kafka topic and the command line ### Walkthrough: `telemetry/admin.py` ```python def client(): return AdminClient({"bootstrap.servers": BOOTSTRAP}) def create_topic(partitions: int = PARTITIONS, retention_hours: int = 168): admin = client() # keep a reference until the futures resolve fut = admin.create_topics([NewTopic(TOPIC, num_partitions=partitions, replication_factor=1, config={"retention.ms": str(retention_hours * 3600 * 1000), "compression.type": "lz4"})]) for name, f in fut.items(): try: f.result() print(f"created topic {name} with {partitions} partitions, retention {retention_hours}h") except Exception as e: # already exists, etc. print(f"{name}: {e}") ``` - `AdminClient({"bootstrap.servers": BOOTSTRAP})` connects to Kafka for management tasks (create, delete, describe topics). `bootstrap.servers` is the first address a client contacts; Kafka then tells it about every broker. - `NewTopic(TOPIC, num_partitions=6, replication_factor=1, config={...})` describes the topic: 6 partitions, 1 copy (one broker locally), 7-day retention in milliseconds, lz4 compression. - `create_topics` is **asynchronous**: it returns a dict of **futures**. `f.result()` waits for the answer and raises if it failed (for example "already exists", which we print and ignore). - `admin = client()` is kept in a variable on purpose. The first version did `client().create_topics(...)`; Python garbage-collected the client before the request finished and the topic was silently not created (F5). > **Python lesson: futures.** A future is a placeholder for a result that arrives later. `future.result()` blocks until it arrives. Whatever object owns the connection must stay alive until then. | Choice | Why | |---|---| | **6 partitions** | Up to 6 consumers read in parallel. Choose for future parallelism: increasing partitions later changes which partition each key maps to and breaks per-engine ordering | | **replication_factor=1** | One broker locally. Production: 3, so a broker can die without data loss | | **retention 168 h** | Replay up to a week after a bug | | **lz4** | Fast compression, less disk and network |
